newsitem.title: USA: Chinese tungsten imports may be short lived-Avocet.
newsitem.headline: Chinese tungsten imports may be short lived-Avocet.

text.p: Imports of tungsten by China, the world's dominant supplier of the hard metal, may be short-lived as domestic producers come to grips with illegal mining and offshore supplies dry up, Robert Bunting, President of Avocet Tungsten, said.

"The APT producers are squirming, and are being forced to try to move their prices up," Bunting said. "Having stamped out illegal mining over the last few months, it forced the price up by about 40 percent for concentrates in China."
Concentrates in China were now fetching about $46 per metric tonne unit, added Bunting. He visited China last week.
Traders in Hong Kong told Reuters last Friday that China was now importing tungsten.
Tungsten in a strategic metal used to make cutting tool steels, light bulb filaments, heavy metal components, and catalysts.

The large Chinese state-owned and small private local tungsten mines are clamping down on illegal mining which fed cheap concentrates to producers of APT or ammonium para-tungstate, an intermediate product.
The big mines also persuaded the Chinese goverment to stockpile surplus concentrates, Bunting said.

The APT producers have been importing concentrates from sources such as the Russian and Kazakh stockpiles in a bid to avoid paying the higher prices for concentrates sold by legitimate Chinese mines, Bunting said.
"To think they can go offshore to buy cheap stuff to whipsaw the Chinese miners is a bit of a lost cause. Russian and Kazakh are in diminishing availability as time goes by," Bunting added.
Avocet is the largest Western world tungsten miner, but all of its output from Portugal and Peruvian mines is fed into the company's APT plant in Bishop, California.
"It's highly unlikely we will be supplying anything to China," Bunting said.

The clampdown on illegal Chinese mining - some of the operations have even been dynamited - has been so successful that the small local mines are now able to seek higher concentrates prices than their bigger, state-owned rivals, Bunting said.
"This reverse is significant and can only happen if the local miners are not being attacked as much by illegal mining," Bunting added.
If the clampdown becomes more successful, "it will just tighten up the market even faster," he said.
China has been importing tungsten in the past two years at about 3,000 tonnes per year of product, Bunting noted.
